newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets weaker after bearish US data.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets weaker after bearish US data.

text.p: World oil markets were weaker on Wednesday after the release of bearish oil data from the United States and confirmation that Iraq's "oil-for-food" deal with the U.N. had been renewed for another six months.
Brent Blend crude, the world benchmark grade, ended the day 18 cents a barrel down at $18.71 a barrel, well under the $19 average of the past three months.
"The market still looks bad, I'm afraid," said one broker at the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) in London.

Oil stocks in the U.S. rose 4.2 million barrels on the week to May 30, while gasoline inventories were 900,000 barrels higher, according to figures released on Wednesday by the U.S. Department of Energy.

The data also showed that U.S. refineries were running at 100.4 percent of nameplate capacity, up from an already high 99.5 percent last week, as they cranked up their output of gasoline after the Memorial Day holiday which traditionally marks the start of the summer driving season.
Gasoline demand in the U.S. is forecast to grow by 2.5 percent this summer and is one of the few bullish factors underpinning the wider oil market.
"I still think gasoline will provide some support. The market has been very much U.S. product-led recently," said Mehdi Varzi, oil analayst at Kleinwort Benson in London.
But he warned "any further gasoline builds should push the price lower" and saw "no shortage of crude oil worldwide".
Confirmation of the U.N.-Iraq deal had little immediate impact on the market because it had been widely anticipated.
The current $2 billion deal, an exception to the economic sanctions in place since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, expires on June 7 and the new 180-day deal will be in force from June 8.
Under its terms Baghdad is allowed to use oil earnings to buy food, medicines and other necessities for ordinary Iraqis who have suffered under sanctions.
